states.name: empty
states.gap: Title carries zero file-type signal — a bare 110px 'Untitled' means a .md and a .txt of the same name render as the identical 8 glyphs in the bar, where A's 48px of '.md' at least disambiguates them at a glance. B's canvas is also 2 levels darker (#F7F7F7 vs #F9F9F9), which drops the #8C8C8C chrome ink to a marginally lower contrast ratio against it.
states.gapTheirs: Title bar prints the filesystem extension: 'Untitled.md' measures 157px where B's 'Untitled' is 110px — 48px of '.md' (x=1459–1506) parked in the one centred slot the bar exists for. Worse, the string is centred as a whole, so the document's actual name spans x=1351–1455 with its optical centre at ~1403, sitting ~37px left of the window's 1440px axis; the name a writer looks for is never on the axis, and drifts further with every longer filename.
states.verdict: This is the same chrome twice — same 26×24 toggle at x=34, same 52×24 View control at x=2794, same #8C8C8C, same 17px stats band with the number at #4A4A4A over the label at #8C8C8C — so the whole judgement collapses onto eleven glyphs versus eight. A's title bar is doing the file manager's job instead of the writer's: '.md' is a fact about storage, not about the piece, and centring the full string leaves the name itself 37px off-axis, which is exactly the kind of drift a typographer sees before they see the word. Neither side draws a hairline anywhere — a single-pixel column at x=2400 runs one flat grey from y=0 to y=1799 in both — so neither bar is actually separated from the page it sits against, and neither pretends to be. B wins on the one thing that differs, and it's a thin win.

states.name: typing
states.gap: The page runs right into the chrome: A's last body line stops 9 device px (4.5 logical) above the stats hairline, against B's 33 device px (16.5 logical) — the rule reads as a lid clamped on the line rather than a bar the page passes under. A's count row is also seated 3 logical px above the bar's optical centre (14 px from the rule, 20 px to the window edge) where B's is 2 px off (15/19).
states.gapTheirs: No weight step between figure and label. For the identical string '188' at identical 17 px cap height, A's digits carry 323 dark pixels / 16,639 ink units against B's 266 / 13,119 — A's numbers are ~21% fatter in stroke, reading semibold against a light label; B's digits are barely heavier than 'words'. The greys are not the differentiator (number #B5B5B5 vs #B6B6B6, label #CECECE vs #CFCFCF, within one level), so B's count is carried on colour alone and the number stops leading its cell.
states.verdict: These two bars are near-clones — same 26 px height, same half-pixel hairline at the same 9-level contrast, same 4 px number-to-label and ~16 px cell-to-cell gutters, both locked to the 1440 px centre axis, both correctly dropping the title bar and leaving the bar ends empty. The one thing that separates them is the thing the bar exists for: A's figures are set heavy enough that the number arrives before the label at a glance, while B's '188' and 'words' read as one grey run you have to parse. Against that, A lets the rule crowd the last line to within 4.5 px, which a writer feels the moment the cursor reaches the bottom of the window. Weak hierarchy in the only row of chrome you kept is a worse failure than a tight bottom gutter, so A — but by a hair, and A owes B a bottom margin.

states.gapTheirs: A's View menu has a broken left text edge. 'Enable Focus Mode', 'Hide Bars' and 'All Commands…' start at x≈34 in a 400 px crop, but 'Sentence', 'Duo', 'Dark Mode' and 'Statistics' start at x≈56. states.verdict: A's menu looks like it was put together by hand: three rows sit a full tick-gutter to the left of their neighbours, and you notice it every time you open the menu to find a setting. B's menu is taller and busier, but every label, separator and key label lines up on a real grid, and the greyed Spell Check row is clearly a quieter grey. B's ticks are clumsy and too heavy, but that is a fault of weight, not of structure. The bars are close to identical, so the menu decides it, and A's menu doesn't hold together.

states.verdict: A puts its menu right on top of the stats bar that opened it, and the bar shows a pressed grey pill, so you can see what you clicked. The tick on 'Hide Statistics' is a lie, though: the menu says the stats are hidden while you're looking at them. B's menu is honest but lands far off to the right over your prose, as if a different control opened it, and its ticks sag below the line. A lie in one row is easier to live with than a menu that appears somewhere else and makes you look for it.

states.verdict: The two stats bars are the same bar: numbers at #4A4A4A over labels at #8C8C8C on both, 33 vs 32 device-px cell gaps, both centred within 1 px of the window midline, neither carrying a hairline. So the whole chrome comparison collapses onto one word, and B loses it — 'Untitled.md' tells a writer neither which piece they are in nor why they should care that it is Markdown. A forfeits most of that win the moment you look below the bar: no caret during a selection, and a wrapped selection line whose fill starts at x=442 against a text column at x=622, hanging a 180 device-px (90 logical px) slab of blue in the empty left margin under nothing at all. Take A for the bar and expect to lose your place in the text every time you select a sentence.
